fetched_contents.text: Financing strategies for the resilience of cultural landscapes. Lessons learned from a systematic literature and practice review 1. Introduction Amidst the urgency of climate change adaptation and mitigation, which often exceeds available public budgets (European Commission, 2022; Rojas, 2016), there is a growing recognition of the vital role played by innovative financing strategies and business models (Allegro et al., 2021). Recent reports by the World Bank and the European Commission demonstrated the economic benefits of investing in disaster resilience, enhancing financial preparedness, and building capacity (World Bank, 2024). In a similar vein, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has recently issued a call for innovative ideas to be included in their upcoming Global Assessment Report 2025, which will focus on “Financing and Investing for Our Future”. Despite this growing interest, the existing body of knowledge on resilience financing for cultural heritage and landscapes is somehow fragmented, and primarily focuses on the conservation or reuse of the built heritage (e.g., Borin & Fantini, 2023; Pickerill, 2021a, Pickerill, 2021b). According to the European Landscape Convention, landscape is defined as “an area, as perceived by people, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors” (Art 1, Council of Europe, 2000). Building on this definition, within RescueMe project1 cultural landscapes (CLs) are understood as “landscapes whose character is the result of the historic action and interaction of natural and human factors with significant cultural significance for the communities that live in them and intrinsic resilience” (Gandini et al., 2023: p.82). Thus, unlike conventional cultural heritage categories such as architectural monuments, archaeological artefacts, and museum collections, productive CLs are dynamic socio-ecological systems. In the context of climate change, resilience is understood as “the ability of a system and its component parts to anticipate, absorb, accommodate, or recover from the effects of a hazardous event in a timely and efficient manner, including through ensuring the preservation, restoration, or improvement of its essential basic structures and functions” (IPCC, 2012, p. 563). In line with this definition, the concept of Resilient Heritage Landscape (RHL), introduced within the RescueME project, seeks to intertwine cultural heritage with nature and community, viewing them through the lens of complex socio-ecological systems (SES). In this view, the resilience of CLs is conceptualised through six capitals, including natural, built, social, financial and human capital, which are linked to a set of key elements. These capitals represent the assets and resources connected to the capacity of communities for prospective development, and aimed at enabling resilience improvements based on coping, adaptive, and transformative capacities of CLs (Gandini et al., 2023). Thus, the resilience of CLs demands a holistic approach that addresses not only the physical dimension but also ensures the continuity of underlying productive activities. Therefore, the resilience of CLs can base on the capacity of stakeholders to virtuously use existing EFB strategies within key sectors or “entry points” for investments, such as agriculture, forestry, tourism, cultural and creative industries (CCIs), among others, as well as their ability to maintain the functions of CLs, including the productive ones (Fig. 1). Few studies have addressed the financial strategies for CLs, focusing on specific case studies (e.g., Gaitán-Cremaschi et al., 2017; Rodríguez et al., 2022). While these studies provide useful insights, they are often limited to region-specific settings, including regulatory and governance frameworks. This study aims to consolidate fragmented knowledge, by mapping empirical patterns of economic, financing and business (EFB) solutions used for the protection of CLs. Based on a systematic review of existing literature, databases, and drawing insights from prior projects, this study presents a thorough review of innovative EFB solutions that have the potential to leverage regenerative capital investments in landscape resilience. It reveals dominant categories of EFB solutions - EFB strategies - that can be used for the resilience of CLs. In addition, it provides the reflection on the complex interrelations of EFB strategies with the landscape resilience, with the aim to offer valuable insights to policymakers, landscape practitioners, and other stakeholders looking to develop EFB strategies, raise awareness and unlock the potential to implement transformative changes towards resilience. This article is structured as follows. In Section 2, the process of systematic literature review is explained in detail. Section 3 reports the main results of the research including descriptive analysis of each EFB strategy identified. The reflection on key benefits associated with EFB strategies and key enabling factors for their implementation are discussed in the Section 4. Finally, conclusions are given in Section 5, including the implications of the results for future research and policies. 2. Methods 2.1. fetched_contents.text: A Blended Finance Framework for Heritage-Led Urban Regeneration 1. Introduction > “Culture is key to what makes cities attractive, creative and sustainable. History shows that culture is at the heart of urban development, evidenced through cultural landmarks, heritage and traditions. Without culture, cities as vibrant life-spaces do not exist; they are merely concrete and steel constructions, prone to social degradation and fracture. It is culture that makes the difference. How can culture be integrated into urban strategies to ensure their sustainability?” > > [1] This statement, in the introduction to the book Culture Urban Future, published by UNESCO in 2016, set the stage within the field of heritage conservation for a wide reconsideration of how it contributes to planetary sustainability and the future of the built environment. Its publication coincided with the inclusion of heritage conservation in the United Nations Sustainable 2030 Development Goals (target 11.4) [2] and in the New Urban Agenda of UN-HABITAT III [3]. The statement speaks to the value we traditionally place on culture as the cohesive, unifying element that holds our communities together through a sense of identity. Today however, culture and heritage have a much larger role to play in the economic life of communities, the control of climate change, and the advancement of social equity that are at the forefront of our concerns. Urban heritage, including tangible and intangible elements, is key to the character of a city or urban area, and comprises one of its principal values. The importance of urban heritage conservation is underscored by the fact that, as of 2019, more than 70% of cultural properties inscribed on the World Heritage List were located in or encompass urban areas, including more than 2,700 cities and towns in 624 out of a total 1092 inscribed properties [4]. Heritage is an important part of the planetary legacy that is presently under threat due to a range of factors including unmanaged and inequitable growth, economic decline in city centers, and the effects of climate change. Failure to integrate these assets into changing urban environments results in irreparable losses to future generations [5]. To integrate concern for the conservation of traditional urban environments into the sustainability agenda, in 2011 the World Heritage Centre developed Historic Urban Landscape (HUL) recommendations for the proper management of change impacting heritage assets. The HUL recommendations call for regulatory systems and financial tools “aimed at building capacities and supporting innovate income-generating development, rooted in tradition [6]”. The most vigorous response to these Recommendations to date comes from the developed world. European policy initiatives in the last few years, such as the 2018 Davos Declaration [7] and the European Union Horizon 2020 program, focused on heritage as a key element in supporting the region’s sense of its core values. Under Horizon 2020, the recently completed EU CLIC program (Circular models Leveraging Investments in Cultural heritage adaptive reuse, i.e.,“ARCH”) produced dozens of research papers as well as demonstration projects. Dr. Tracy Pickerill of Technical University Dublin contributed an overview of financial and nonfinancial instruments and investment leverage enablers for cultural heritage adaptive reuse. The paper presents a toolkit to help urban authorities understand how to create a blended pool of capital and leverage enablers. It also collects dozens of evidence-based examples of collaborative heritage revitalization financing initiatives at all scales [8]. Another CLIC report, by professors Gillian Foster of the Vienna University of Economics and Business and Ruba Saleh of the ICHEC Brussels Management School, develops a cultural heritage index to measure investment opportunities in adaptive reuse across European cities. This index applies 15 indicators in three dimensions (cultural stock, environmental stewardship, and socioeconomic factors) to create a composite indicator, and then evaluates 190 European cities against it. Meaningful for the study is the outcome: the top 20 indexed cities were within seven Western European countries. Ninety percent have at least one World Heritage site within their perimeter, and many are European capitals and hence, historical centers of wealth and culture. The article also presents a compelling summation of how Adaptive Reuse of Cultural Heritage (ARCH) contributes to circular development, as follows Adaptive Reuse of Cultural Heritage: * Extends the lifespan of existing buildings and slows the extraction of natural resources and energy use for new buildings; * Capitalizes on local authenticity; * Supports legal protections that often come with governmental financial commitments and incentives; * Preserves cultural, emotional, social, and physical values. Reaching sustainability goals in areas with rich architectural heritage will be difficult without Adaptive Reuse of Cultural Heritage (ARCH) [9]. The extension of this research and indexing to other parts of the world will provide an opportunity to evaluate the readiness of a city to embark upon a heritage regeneration initiative and to commit the personnel and resources needed to implement such a program. fetched_contents.text: Financial Sustainability of Cultural Heritage: A Review of Crowdfunding in Europe 1. Introduction The meaning of culture has matured from representing artistic expression with no economic value to becoming a public good and a force of economic change (Manda et al. 2017). However, processes of preservation, protection, regular operating, and maintenance of cultural heritage are expensive and typically require financial resources, which are often difficult to obtain. Therefore, to increase the likelihood of funding, cultural projects need to demonstrate economic and financial sustainability (Eppich and Grinda 2019). Economic sustainability is generally defined as the “process of allocating and protecting scarce resources while ensuring positive social and environmental outcomes” as well as intergenerational equity (i.e., meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the needs of future generations) (Doane and MacGillivray 2001, p. 16). Therefore, when applied to culture, the economic sustainability of a cultural project refers to the project’s ability to accumulate profit for the general economy. Financial sustainability generally imputes the fiscal ability to continue current policies and service delivery after the funding terminates (Subires and Bolivar 2017). Hybrid instruments blend grant and loan features by combining non-repayable public support with conditional repayment obligations. The evidence here points to a broad family of hybrid financial instruments that are not simply debt or equity but mix features of both. One source defines hybrid financing as where debt and equity meet in the middle, offering investors the potential benefits of both [N1-R1]. Another source explicitly identifies a convertible grant as a hybrid capital instrument with grant-like structure but hybrid capital character [N1-R2]. A broader definition says hybrid financial instruments blend characteristics of both equity and debt markets [N1-R3], while a more general definition treats hybrid financing as any transaction that includes multiple asset class structures in a single transaction [N1-R5]. Taken together, these sources support a practical view of hybrid instruments as instruments that may be partly repayable and partly non-repayable, with eligibility and repayment terms that distinguish them from pure grants.

Specific instrument types that blend grant and loan features include convertible grants, risk-sharing loans with private co-financing, and blended capital pools. [N4-R1], which is a clear hybrid structure because the public entity shares risk and the private co-funder gets a share of the grants corresponding to its contribution. ### 6) Implementation and evaluation evidence

Implementation and evaluation evidence for hybrid heritage instruments suggests both successful deployments and notable challenges. The strongest evidence in the provided sources is a systematic literature and practice review on financing strategies for the resilience of cultural landscapes, which reports that hybrid or blended funding strategy was used in 14.7% of cases, typically based on a mix of financial instruments such as grants, loans (debt), and other instruments [N3-R2]. Another source in the same review notes that public funding comes in the form of grants, combination of a grant and private funding (repayable funding), and public funding with repayable components [N3-R4]. These examples indicate that hybrid financing is not yet universal in cultural heritage, but it is being actively used and studied.

Successful deployments are illustrated by the CLIC project’s blended finance framework for heritage-led urban regeneration. This framework is described as a toolkit to help urban authorities create a blended pool of capital and leverage enablers, and it collects dozens of evidence-based examples of collaborative heritage revitalization financing initiatives at all scales [N4-F2]. The CLIC report also notes that the ARCH project produced dozens of research papers and demonstration projects, showing that hybrid financing can be deployed in concrete, operational ways [N4-F2]. The same source emphasizes that adaptive reuse supports legal protections, governmental financial commitments, and incentives, and that it contributes to circular development by extending building lifespans and preserving local authenticity [N4-F2]. These examples suggest that when hybrid instruments are well designed and implemented, they can create meaningful outcomes for heritage projects.

Problematic deployments are more thinly documented in the provided evidence, but the literature review does highlight that the body of knowledge on resilience financing for cultural heritage is fragmented and often limited to region-specific settings and regulatory frameworks [N3-F1]. It also notes that there is little progress toward integrated coordination between government agencies or multilateral public-private co-financing and blended capital projects as a strategy for sustainable development [N3-F1]. This implies that hybrid financing can be difficult to implement at scale because it requires coordination across institutions, clear governance structures, and alignment of different funding modalities. The review also states that cities resetting their agendas after the global pandemic may face challenges in implementing heritage regeneration initiatives, especially in developing countries [N3-F1]. These points suggest that while hybrid instruments can work well in some contexts, their implementation can be problematic when coordination is weak or when local capacities are limited.

Measures used to assess effectiveness and sustainability include financial sustainability indicators, performance outcomes, and governance conditions. The financial sustainability review defines financial sustainability as the project’s ability to continue after funding ends, including enough resources to meet operating and maintenance obligations [N5-F3]. It also identifies five categories of financial sustainability: revenue identification, expenditure analysis, administration and reporting, strategic planning, and alignment and support of the mission [N5-F3]. The literature review also reports that hybrid financing strategies are evaluated in the context of climate change adaptation, disaster resilience, and broader landscape resilience [N3-F1]. In the heritage context, the CLIC report links financial instruments to income-generating development rooted in tradition [N4-F2], and the ARCH discussion links adaptive reuse to extended building lifespans, local authenticity, and preserved values [N4-F2]. These measures suggest that effectiveness is not judged solely by whether a project is funded, but by whether it continues, delivers intended outcomes, and aligns with broader resilience goals.

Lessons for policymakers and funders include the need for blended capital pools, strong governance, and flexible, outcome-based conditions. The CLIC report states that blended capital projects are needed to create a blended pool of capital and leverage enablers, and that the toolkit helps urban authorities understand how to create such pools [N4-F2]. The same source also emphasizes that heritage conservation projects need to meet investor requirements concerning risk reduction and proof of positive impact [N4-F2]. The literature review further notes that the existing body of knowledge is fragmented and often limited to region-specific settings, implying that successful policy design requires attention to local context and coordination [N3-F1]. The financial sustainability review adds that crowdfunding suitability for cultural heritage projects depends on the policy framework, heritage project nature, and campaign management [N5-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that policymakers and funders should prioritize blended financing structures, outcome-based repayment conditions, and governance arrangements that can support long-term sustainability and coordination across public and private actors [N4-F2][N5-F3].

### Conclusion

Hybrid financial instruments integrate grants and loans by combining immediate non-repayable support with conditional repayment or performance-linked obligations. They are especially well suited to cultural heritage projects because they address long-term investment needs, reduce reliance on pure grants, and allow for risk sharing and flexible repayment tied to outcomes. The legal and tax framework supports this by treating hybrid instruments as combinations of debt and equity under IFRS/GAAP, distinguishing grants from repayable instruments through repayment obligations, and using tax mechanisms to support repayable components [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R4][N6-R1]. Implementation evidence shows that hybrid instruments can be successful when blended capital pools, governance, and outcome-based conditions are in place, but they can also be challenging when coordination is weak or when local capacities are limited [N3-F1][N4-F2]. Overall, hybrid financing helps cultural heritage projects by preserving public support, engaging private capital, and aligning repayment with project performance and sustainability goals [N4-F2][N5-R2].
